results.summary_before: This design implements a 24-hour digital clock with separate BCD outputs for two hour digits and two minute digits. It uses a 1 MHz reference clock and provides a set button to cycle through the digits and a pulse input to advance the selected digit. External hardware includes three push buttons, a 1 MHz signal generator, and four 7-segment BCD decoders to display the time. The design is a straightforward clock with no unusual features or silicon test results reported.

results.summary_before: Underserved is a Tiny Tapeout implementation of SERV, a compact RISC-V CPU that boots from an external SPI flash memory in XIP mode and executes instructions directly from it. It provides GPIO pins that can be used for various purposes, such as bitbanged UART, and uses SPI pins for flash communication. The design expects a compatible SPI flash memory and can be tested using a testbench with a flash model, with FuseSoC used for simulation and linting. The documentation is thorough, describing the boot process and test setup, but no silicon results are reported.

results.summary_before: This design implements a countdown timer that uses three rotary encoders to adjust seven-segment display values and PWM brightness. It includes debouncing logic and a control pin to enable a minute-based countdown, and it requires a 16 MHz clock oscillator. To use it, external hardware including a PMOD, three seven-segment LED displays, and three digital encoders must be connected to the appropriate pins. The design was created as a term project for the Zero to ASIC course, and its functionality is straightforward but relies on external components for interaction.

results.summary_before: This project renders a 3D torus (donut) on a VGA display using a raymarching technique with a CORDIC unit to calculate distances. It runs at a non-standard 1220x480 resolution and uses spatial and temporal dithering to improve appearance despite low horizontal resolution. It requires a 48 MHz clock and a Tiny VGA Pmod for video output. Silicon tests show it works but may have minor glitches at 48 MHz; running at 45 MHz avoids them.
